You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

steps.text:
Demo: output is input shifted down by 1 row? Compare: input row0 "777", output row0 "777". Input rows: r0=777, r1=877, r2=888... output: r0=777, r1=777, r2=877, r3=888, r4=888... Input r1=877 appears at output r2; input r2=888 at output r3,r4? Input r2=888, r3=888; output r3=888, r4=888. So it's a shift down by 1 with wrap? Input last rows 7's shifted... input r14=777 output r14=777. Let me check: shift down by 1: output[i]=input[i-1]. output r1 = input r0 =777 ✓. output r2=input r1=877 ✓. output r3=input r2=888 ✓, r4=input r3=888 ✓, r5=input r4=778 ✓... output r5 = "778"? given output row5: 7 7 8 ✓. Then output r14 = input r13=777 ✓. So rule: shift down by one row (top row stays? no—output r0=777=input r0, could be wrap: output r0 = input r14 =777, also works). Same grid size.

Test: 6x21 grid, shift down by 1. Rows of test: r0 all... test row5 vs row4 differ, so shifting matters. Wrap or drop? In demo, input r0=777 = input r14=777, ambiguous. For test, top row of output: if drop and fill with... the padding? If wrap, output r0 = input r5. If drop-and-copy, output r0=input r0.

Hmm. Common ARC task "shift down, output r0 = r0"? Actually simplest: output = [input[0]] + input[:-1]? That matches demo (r0 unchanged). Alternatively circular shift also matches demo. Which is more likely? In demo both are identical because r0==r14. Consider: maybe the rule is each row shifts down by 1 cyclically. Or maybe it's gravity? No—nonzero cells moving down?

Look: it's a full-row down shift. I'll guess circular shift down by 1? Hmm. Alternatively "output row i = input row i-1, output row 0 = input row 0" (pad by repeating first row). Test r0 vs r5: r0 = 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 7 0 7 7 7 0 7 7 7 7 7 0 0; r5 = 0 0 0 0 0 0 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 7 0 7 0 0 0 0. Different, so choice matters.

Think: another demo would disambiguate (cost 1). We have 8 attempts, plenty. But wrong submission only costs 1 too and gives feedback. Budget: unsolved=16; correct costs submissions+demos. If I submit wrong (cost1) then still need correct. Getting another demo (cost1) tells which shift rule. Either way similar cost. But wrong submission gives no info about why. Request demo 2 to disambiguate.

Demo 2: output row0 = all 9s (the background color), rows shift down by 1, last row of input is dropped (not wrapped — since input r7 has 8s but output r0 is all 9s). Wait, output r7 = input r6? Check: input r6 = "9...9 8 8 9 9 9 8 9 9 9 9" vs output r7 = "9 9 9 9 9 9 9 9 9 8 8 8 8 8 8 8 8 8 8 9 9 9 8 9 9 9 9" = input r6 ✓. And output r7 = input r6, so input r7 dropped, r0 replaced by background (most common color / the color of the majority? Here output r0 is all 9). Background color = most common in input.

For test: background = 0. Output = row of all 0s + input rows 0..4.
Demo 2 resolves it: shift down by one row; the top row becomes all background (the grid's dominant color), and the input's last row is dropped. Applying to the test grid with background 0.
